stories.body: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard says seven oil tankers were damaged or disabled in the Strait of Hormuz, including four that it says caught fire while transferring oil and three that struck mines. The claims have not been independently verified, and US Central Command rejects the mine account, saying shipping lanes have been cleared and Iran is using missiles and drones against vessels. Tehran warned that it could target US bases if Washington expands escorts for commercial shipping, while reports also point to possible further US and Israeli strikes on Iranian military and energy-related targets.
stories.headline: Iran conflict risks widening as Tehran reports tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz

stories.body: A magnitude-7 earthquake struck a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet late Thursday, killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing at least 339 homes, according to Chinese officials. More than 1,600 local rescue personnel have been deployed, with tents, prefabricated housing, beds and winter clothing sent to the area as residents face subzero temperatures and the risk of aftershocks. The US Geological Survey recorded at least seven aftershocks, while authorities reported disrupted communications, rockfalls and rail-service precautions.
stories.headline: Magnitude-7 earthquake in Tibet kills at least 16 and destroys hundreds of homes

stories.body: A BBC investigation documents at least 43 attacks on hospitals and other health-care sites in el-Fasher between May 2024 and October 2025, concluding that Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces systematically helped destroy the city’s health system during its siege and takeover. The BBC’s data also records 120 medical workers injured, 55 killed and 10 abducted or forcibly disappeared during the wider conflict period. The RSF’s health minister rejected the allegations as propaganda, but the UN human rights chief said the reported attacks could constitute serious violations of international humanitarian law and potentially war crimes.
stories.headline: BBC investigation finds Sudan’s RSF fighters deliberately targeted hospitals in el-Fasher

stories.body: New polling before Sunday’s Brazilian presidential runoff shows the race between left-wing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro tightening into a statistical tie. Surveys cited by local reporting put Bolsonaro’s earlier edge at less than a point or show the candidates level, following a contentious televised debate and a late campaign push by Lula. The election has major implications for Brazil’s democratic direction and for Amazon policy, as Bolsonaro supporters in the northern state of Roraima hope for a return to mining-friendly policies while Indigenous activists prepare to resist them.
stories.headline: Brazil’s presidential runoff remains too close to call as Lula faces Flávio Bolsonaro

stories.body: Thousands of Venezuelans protested in Caracas and other cities to demand free elections and political change, in the opposition’s first nationwide mobilization in nearly two years. No date has been set for a vote to choose a successor to Nicolás Maduro, who was captured by US forces in January, and opposition leader María Corina Machado has called for elections by July 2027. Interim president Delcy Rodríguez has said elections will be held, but her socialist government remains in power as negotiations over electoral and judicial reforms proceed slowly.
stories.headline: Venezuelans hold first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years

stories.body: Senate Majority PAC, Democrats’ principal Senate-focused super PAC, says it raised $354 million through October 14, surpassing its previous full-cycle record from 2024. The group had $32.7 million on hand and says it is spending across battleground states through Election Day. Republicans’ Senate Leadership Fund remains ahead in total fundraising, reporting more than $423 million as of September 30, helped by a $158 million third-quarter contribution from Elon Musk, but Democratic candidates have raised strongly enough to narrow the outside-money advantage in some races.
stories.headline: Democrats’ top Senate super PAC reports record $354 million fundraising haul

stories.body: New York City Council voted 40-7 to phase out the city’s horse-drawn carriage industry, allowing drivers to continue operating until June 2028 while the city develops transition support and job-placement programs. Supporters of the ban cited longstanding animal-welfare concerns and a fatal accident involving an 18-year-old tourist earlier this year. Carriage drivers and their union oppose the measure, arguing that it threatens independent businesses and does not guarantee compensation for carriage licenses; the Transport Workers Union says it plans to challenge the law in court.
stories.headline: New York City votes to end horse-drawn carriages by 2028

stories.body: Georgia Republicans are relying heavily on wealthy political newcomer Rick Jackson’s gubernatorial campaign to keep the state competitive as party leaders worry about losses elsewhere on the ticket. Jackson, a billionaire health-care executive, has spent nearly $200 million and remains in a close race with Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, while Republican Senate candidate Mike Collins trails Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff in polling. GOP strategists say Jackson must appeal simultaneously to moderates uncomfortable with President Donald Trump and to Trump’s base, making Georgia a test of whether heavy spending can offset an unfavorable national political environment.
stories.headline: Georgia Republicans look to Rick Jackson to limit broader midterm losses

stories.body: People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo has placed Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo second and Borja Sémper third on his Madrid congressional list for Spain’s November 29 general election. Álvarez de Toledo’s promotion from sixth place is widely seen as an effort to strengthen the party’s harder-edged wing as it competes with Vox, while Sémper represents a more moderate current within the party. The broader candidate-list overhaul combines prominent ideological spokespeople with experienced regional officials and mayors as Feijóo prepares a potential governing team.
stories.headline: Spain’s PP elevates Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo and Borja Sémper on Feijóo’s Madrid ticket

stories.body: Three Spanish citizens living abroad who obtained nationality under Spain’s Democratic Memory Law have asked the Supreme Court to lift a precautionary measure that prevents some newly naturalized citizens from voting in the upcoming election. The court suspended the electoral effect of census registrations for people naturalized through the so-called grandchildren’s law, except those who can document an ancestor’s exile, while it considers a dispute over electoral authority. Lawyers for the affected citizens argue that the measure effectively suspends a fundamental right to vote, treats citizens differently depending on where they live, and was imposed before those affected could participate in the case.
stories.headline: Citizens affected by Spain’s ‘grandchildren’s law’ challenge suspension of voting rights

stories.body: Spain’s Civil Guard arrested two people linked to migrant-aid organizations in Ceuta and is investigating others over allegations that pepper spray and bladed weapons were distributed to migrants and that migrants were encouraged to attack security forces. Officers searched premises used by No Name Kitchen and mutual-aid groups near the Tarajal border area. The organizations deny the accusations, saying their work is limited to humanitarian assistance and documenting possible rights violations, while the police investigation remains open and authorities have not publicly detailed the evidence behind the allegations.
stories.headline: Spanish police arrest two Ceuta aid workers over alleged distribution of pepper spray and weapons

stories.body: Catalonia’s Mossos d’Esquadra have identified 34 violent youth groups involving about 1,000 people and will launch the Proa plan in November to prevent, investigate and dismantle them. Police say the most active groups, including Trinitarios, Barrio 18 and Los 300, account for most reported incidents and operate mainly in Barcelona and its metropolitan area, with branches elsewhere in Catalonia. Officials say the groups are more culturally diverse and less rigidly hierarchical than the Latin gangs of the early 2000s, but are linked to assaults, robbery, drug trafficking and at least three homicides in recent years.
stories.headline: Catalan police launch plan against youth gangs after identifying 34 groups

stories.body: Barcelona plans to open a new underground stormwater reservoir at Rambla de Prim in 2028, its first such facility since 2013, after exceptionally heavy rainfall earlier this month pushed the city’s existing network to its limits. The 15 current reservoirs can collectively hold roughly 450,000 to 477,000 cubic meters of water, and several reached capacity during the October 3-4 storms. The new facility is expected to hold about 60,000 to 100,000 cubic meters, depending on the cited project figures, and is part of a wider effort to add reservoirs, expand drainage capacity and make streetscapes more permeable as intense rainfall becomes more common.
stories.headline: Barcelona plans first new stormwater reservoir in 15 years for 2028 opening

stories.body: Ferrocarrils de la Generalitat de Catalunya has not set a date to restore normal service on the R5, R6, S8 and S3 lines after part of the Gornal tunnel ceiling collapsed in L’Hospitalet de Llobregat. Trains are operating on a single track through the affected section, with the R5 and R6 cut to two trains an hour and terminating at L’Hospitalet-Avinguda Carrilet rather than Plaça Espanya; the S3 is further reduced, while the S8 is running about every 15 minutes. Initial investigations have ruled out nearby Adif infrastructure as the cause, and work is focused on stabilizing the tunnel before both tracks reopen.
stories.headline: FGC services remain disrupted after Gornal tunnel ceiling collapse

stories.body: Barcelona’s scheduled bus strike has been called off after TMB management and unions reached a preliminary four-year collective agreement. The deal provides for additional rest days, more weekend time off and a gradual reduction of the working week to 35 hours, with bus workers set to receive 10 additional rest days next year and potentially three more under specified conditions. The agreement cancels the partial stoppages that had been planned for this week and five additional days in October.
stories.headline: Barcelona bus strike is called off after TMB and unions reach pre-agreement

stories.body: Catalonia’s labour inspectorate has found that Barcelona’s municipal Parks and Gardens service operates 105 vehicles without air conditioning, concluding that working conditions do not meet minimum safety requirements during extreme heat. The vehicles include 67 vans, 27 pickup trucks, 10 trucks and one car, and both management and worker representatives acknowledged that staff using them in summer are exposed to high interior temperatures. Following a union complaint, inspectors ordered the municipal company to correct the deficiencies; the city says it has invested in climate control for 58% of the fleet and is considering further upgrades.
stories.headline: Labour inspectors find 105 Barcelona parks-and-gardens vehicles lack air conditioning
